title: How Often Does "Hell" Appear?
hook: The KJV says 'hell' 54 times, Young's Literal Translation never. Which one is the Bible?
tldr: 'Hell' is an English word, not a Hebrew or Greek one. Translators used it for four different words: Sheol, Hades, Gehenna and Tartarus. So the count swings from 54 in the KJV to about 13 in modern versions and zero in literal ones like Young's, Rotherham's and the Septuagint.
big_idea: One English word covers four different biblical words and places.

points.title: Hell is an English word
points.text: The video stresses that 'hell' does not occur in the Hebrew or Greek. It is a translators' choice for several distinct words, so the real question is which word stands behind each English 'hell'.

points.title: 54 or 13 or zero
points.text: The KJV uses 'hell' 54 times (31 Old Testament, 23 New). The NKJV has 32, the NASB, NIV and ESV about 13-14, and Young's Literal, Rotherham, Weymouth and the Concordant versions none at all.

points.title: Four words, not one place
points.text: Sheol and Hades mean the grave or realm of all the dead. Gehenna is a real valley outside Jerusalem. Tartarus appears once, for imprisoned angels. The video says hell is 'a place or places', not one place.

points.title: Hell for the wicked, grave for the righteous
points.text: The KJV split Sheol 31 times 'hell', 31 'grave', 3 'pit'. The video notes the pattern: the wicked go to 'hell', but Jacob goes to 'the grave'. One Hebrew word, two very different English pictures.

points.title: Hell once meant 'covered'
points.text: English 'hell' comes from Old English hel, from Proto-Germanic haljo, 'concealed place', tied to a verb meaning to cover or hide. The video links it to 'helling' potatoes, burying them in the ground.

points.title: Jesus holds the keys
points.text: The video rejects 'God sends no one; people send themselves'. No verse says that. Instead the risen Jesus holds the keys of death and Hades, so only he can open or shut it.

sections.h: Why hell is the elephant in the room
sections.summary: The video says that once you grasp God's goodness, hell becomes a huge question. It rejects the popular line that God sends no one to hell and people send themselves: no verse says it, and Jesus holds the keys of death and hell. The view of hell has nothing to do with salvation, so believers should not divide over it.

sections.h: Hell missing from the early gospel
sections.summary: The video notes the apostles' sermons in Acts never mention heaven or hell; making the gospel about the afterlife is recent. God warned Adam only of death, not endless torture. Paul, handling the Corinthian man with his stepmother, said hand him over for destruction of the flesh so his spirit may be saved, with no word of eternal fire.

sections.h: Eternal torment is a view, not hell itself
sections.summary: The video insists it believes in a biblical hell, perhaps more than many, but says eternal conscious torment is one view of hell, not hell itself. Several views exist. Hell, it says, is a place or places, three different ones, to be traced word by word.

sections.h: Where the English word came from
sections.summary: Old English hel comes from Proto-Germanic haljo, 'concealed place, underworld', from a verb meaning to cover or hide, with cousins like Dutch hel, German Holle and Gothic halja. In Norse myth Hel, Loki's daughter, rules the dead. The video ties it to 'helling' potatoes, burying seed, and helmet; Webster's derived it from helan, to cover.

sections.h: Hell as darkness and as a mindset
sections.summary: Because the word means concealed, the video says burying someone in a casket was 'sending them to hell', covering them up. It applies this spiritually too: living concealed in the kingdom of darkness is a kind of hell, and awakening to Christ removes the veil and moves us into the kingdom of light. Hell is places, but often a mindset.

The video's whole-Bible figures: KJV 54, NKJV 32, RSV 12, NASB 13, NIV 13; for the New Testament: KJV 23, NKJV 13, RSV 13, NASB 13, NIV 14. Web tables confirm KJV 54 (31 OT, 23 NT) and NKJV 32 (19 OT, 13 NT). Sources split on the NIV, 13 or 14. The ESV has about 14 and the NLT about 17.

The video says literal Bibles, such as Young's Literal Translation, Rotherham's Emphasized Bible and Weymouth, have 'hell' zero times. So does the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament Jesus and the apostles read, which puts Hades for Sheol. Web tables agree: Young's, Rotherham (1902), Weymouth (1903) and the Concordant Literal New Testament use it 0 times.

Gehenna, the video says, is always rendered 'hell' in older versions, though some newer translations keep 'Gehenna' or 'Valley of Hinnom'. That is better: we do not translate Gethsemane as 'hell', but keep it as the name of a real place. The video calls 'hell' for Gehenna a gross mistranslation.

sections.h: Did Jesus talk most about hell?
sections.summary: The video lists common Bible words: heaven 644, father 944, evil 657, law 599, soul 496, death 456, sin 441, kingdom 384, judgment 344, while an original-language word 'hell' appears zero times. Web counts for 'heaven' vary by version, about 550-583 in the KJV. The claim that Jesus spoke of hell more than anything is called a fallacy.

Sheol means the grave, the realm of the dead, the pit, the underworld. Concordances count it 65 times; the KJV renders it hell 31, grave 31 and pit 3 (the video says 64, with 32, 29 and 3). The video notes the KJV chose 'hell' for the wicked but 'grave' for the righteous, which should make readers pause.

The video adds an aside: Scripture says the righteous and the wicked, just and unjust, all stand before God, who is in heaven. So in that sense everyone goes to heaven at some point. What happens after is up to Jesus, the only judge, and the video admits no one really knows.

sections.h: Samuel and Saul in the same place
sections.summary: In 1 Samuel 28, the dead Samuel is brought up and tells Saul, 'Tomorrow you and your sons will be with me.' The righteous prophet and the rebellious king share Sheol, with no mention of fire. Jews believed the dead slept with their fathers there until the Messiah broke open its gates.

sections.h: The gates of Hades at Caesarea Philippi
sections.summary: The video places Jesus' words 'the gates of Hades shall not prevail' at Caesarea Philippi, by the cave called the gate of Pan. Months later, it says, Jesus broke through those gates: he went into the grave, preached to the dead, emptied it and led captivity captive. Righteous and wicked were both there.

Sheol began morally neutral, the video says, but changed because people felt it unfair that righteous and wicked shared it. Humans prefer retribution, eye for eye, while Jesus taught love of enemies and rebuked James and John for wanting fire from heaven. God's justice aims at restoration, not retribution.

Job wishes he had died at birth, to lie quiet and asleep with kings and counselors. There the wicked cease from troubling, the weary rest, prisoners hear no oppressor, small and great lie together and the slave is free. Job even asks God to hide him in Sheol as a refuge.

David says that if he makes his bed in Sheol, God is there. The video concludes hell cannot be a place void of God's presence or total separation from him; such a place would be a god to itself. Nothing exists apart from the God who upholds all things.

In Eastern culture, the video says, justice was restorative and reflexive: actions bring their own consequences, sowing and reaping. Zechariah defines true justice as mercy and compassion to one's brother, protecting widow, orphan, foreigner and poor. So God's vengeance is the outworking of a justice that restores.

David says God brought his soul up from Sheol, translated 'grave' because the righteous David could not leave 'hell'. If God brought him up, the video argues, Sheol is not permanent. Korah's rebellion is the first time Sheol is a place of punishment. Tyre goes down to the pit amid deep waters, not fire.

Ezekiel 18 and 32 begin separating righteous and wicked, but with no punishment inflicted. The video says afterlife punishment entered Jewish thought only a few centuries before Jesus, under Platonic thought and Greek myth, with hints first in Daniel. Persians, Egyptians and Greeks already pictured burning fire after death.

sections.h: Hades: Greek word and Greek god
sections.summary: Hades, the grave or realm of the dead, is the Greek equivalent of Sheol, used only a handful of times, mainly in Old Testament quotes. The KJV renders it hell in 10 of 11 uses. Hades is also a god: with Zeus and Poseidon he overthrew the Titans and imprisoned them in Tartarus, then ruled the underworld.

sections.h: Gehenna: a valley you can visit
sections.summary: Gehenna is Ge Hinnom, the Valley of Hinnom, also called Tophet, southwest of Jerusalem. It appears 12 times in the New Testament, 11 in Jesus' sayings and once in James. To Jews it was a real place of judgment here and now, known for evil acts including child sacrifice.

Many teach Gehenna was Jerusalem's burning dump, but the video notes the earliest source is a rabbi around 1200 AD, so it will not teach it as fact. It says crucified criminals' bodies may have been thrown there, which is why Joseph of Arimathea begged for Jesus' body.

If someone tells you to go to hell, the video jokes, ask: which one? If they mean Gehenna, ask for about $4,000 for the trip to Jerusalem, where the valley is now a park full of flowers where people barbecue. Its fire and worm were already pictures of death for first-century Jews.

When we read 'hell', the video says, we picture Dante's Inferno and screeching demons, images shaped by movies, mythology, books and plays. Most Jews hearing Jesus would not have pictured that. The video ends by promising Tartarus next and urging viewers to study for themselves.

sections.h: Tyndale and the King James tradition
sections.summary: Tyndale's 1526 New Testament used 'hell' for both Hades (Luke 16) and Gehenna (Matthew 5:22), though he noted they differ. The KJV, largely built on Tyndale, kept 'hell' for Sheol, Hades and Gehenna. The English Revised Version of the 1880s put 'Hades' wherever the Greek has Hades, and modern versions largely followed.

Tartarus appears only in 2 Peter 2:4, as a verb, tartaroo, for angels who sinned being held in chains of darkness until judgment. Traditional writers see a holding place below Hades; others see restraint until judgment. Most modern versions still render it 'hell', part of their roughly 13 uses.

KJV-only writers argue modern versions remove 'hell' and weaken the doctrine. Critics answer that versions like the NASB and ESV still keep 'hell' for Gehenna and Tartarus. Traditional dictionaries also note Hades sometimes means only the grave, so the counts themselves do not settle the doctrine.

mythfact.myth: The word 'hell' is in the original Hebrew and Greek Bible.
mythfact.fact: 'Hell' is an English word. Translators used it for Sheol, Hades, Gehenna and Tartarus, four different words, which is why literal versions never use it.

mythfact.myth: Hell is one single place of fire.
mythfact.fact: The words point to different things: the grave of all the dead, a real valley near Jerusalem, and a prison for angels. The video speaks of hell as places, plural.

mythfact.myth: Every Bible mentions hell about as often.
mythfact.fact: Counts run from 54 in the KJV to 32 in the NKJV, about 13-14 in the NASB, NIV and ESV, and zero in Young's Literal Translation.

mythfact.myth: Jesus talked about hell more than anything else.
mythfact.fact: Gehenna appears 11 times in Jesus' sayings, while words like heaven, father, kingdom and death each appear hundreds of times in the Bible.

terms.meaning: Hebrew word for the grave or realm of the dead, where righteous and wicked alike go.
Greek word for the unseen realm of the dead; the Septuagint uses it for Sheol. Also the Greek god of the underworld.
Greek form of Ge Hinnom, the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, a real place linked with child sacrifice and judgment.
In Greek myth the deepest prison, where the Titans were held. In 2 Peter 2:4 a verb for confining sinning angels.
The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament read by Jesus' contemporaries and the apostles. It renders Sheol as Hades.
An 1862 word-for-word English Bible by Robert Young. It never uses the word 'hell'.

quotes.text: If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there.
I am he that liveth, and was dead; and, behold, I am alive for evermore, Amen; and have the keys of hell and of death.

verses.role: KJV: the wicked 'turned into hell'. The Hebrew is Sheol, the same word used for Jacob.
Jacob's gray hair goes down to Sheol, rendered 'grave' because a patriarch could not go to 'hell'.
Another Sheol verse for righteous Jacob, again translated 'the grave'.
Samuel tells Saul, 'you and your sons will be with me': righteous and wicked share Sheol.
In Sheol the wicked cease troubling and the weary rest: a place of rest, not torment.
If I make my bed in Sheol, God is there: hell is not a place without God.
God brought David's soul up from Sheol, so Sheol is not permanent.
The gates of Hades, spoken at Caesarea Philippi, will not hold against Christ's church.
Jesus holds the keys of death and Hades; people do not send themselves there.
The only use of Tartarus, a verb for confining sinning angels until judgment.

quiz.q: How many times does the KJV use the word 'hell'?
quiz.why: The KJV has 'hell' 54 times, 31 in the Old Testament and 23 in the New, because it used one English word for four original words.

quiz.q: Which translation never uses the word 'hell'?
quiz.why: Young's Literal, like Rotherham, Weymouth, the Concordant version and the Greek Septuagint, keeps the original words and uses 'hell' zero times.

quiz.q: What did the Old English word behind 'hell' originally mean?
quiz.why: Old English hel goes back to Proto-Germanic haljo, a concealed place, from a verb meaning to cover or hide.

reflect: When you read 'hell' in your Bible, do you know which word it translates, and does that change what you picture?

objections.claim: Modern versions cut 'hell' to soften the Bible's warnings.
objections.strongest: The KJV warned of hell 54 times; the NIV and NASB about 13. KJV-only writers argue this drift tracks a culture uncomfortable with judgment and weakens the church's urgency in calling sinners to repent.
objections.response: The drop comes almost entirely from Sheol and Hades, which mean the grave or realm of all the dead. Even Tyndale noted Hades and Gehenna differ, and the English Revised Version restored 'Hades' in the 1880s. Conservative versions like the NASB and ESV still use 'hell' for Gehenna and Tartarus. The change reflects better precision, not a softer doctrine; literal versions from the 1800s went further and dropped 'hell' entirely.

objections.claim: Saying 'hell isn't in the Hebrew or Greek' is a word game; no English word is.
objections.strongest: Every English word in the Bible is a translation. If Gehenna names a place of final judgment, 'hell' is a fair English equivalent, and noting that the word is English proves nothing about the doctrine.
objections.response: True, and the video does not deny a real hell; it says it believes in a biblical hell. The point is that one English word merges four distinct terms. When Sheol, the grave of everyone, Gehenna, a valley outside Jerusalem, and Tartarus share one label, readers import Dante's single fiery underworld into all of them. Counting the words exposes that merger, so each can be read on its own terms.

objections.claim: The KJV used 'hell' or 'grave' for Sheol by context, not bias.
objections.strongest: Sheol is sometimes linked to the wicked, as in Psalm 9:17 and Korah's fall. Choosing 'hell' where the wicked are in view and 'grave' elsewhere is ordinary contextual translation.
objections.response: The Old Testament itself puts righteous and wicked together in Sheol: Samuel tells Saul 'you will be with me', Job calls it rest for all, and David finds God there and is brought up from it. Splitting one word into 'hell' for the wicked and 'grave' for the righteous inserts a distinction the text does not make, and turns a neutral realm of the dead into a place of torment.
